title: Queue-Stack Interconversion
summary: Building a queue out of two stacks (and vice versa) and reasoning about the amortized cost of doing so — a classic test of amortized-analysis intuition, not just implementation.

slides.markdown:
Building a queue out of two stacks (or a stack out of two queues) is a classic interview question precisely because the naive implementation looks like it should cost O(n) per operation — and yet a smarter accounting shows it's O(1) **amortized**. The gap between those two answers is what's actually being tested.

The underlying trick in both directions is the same: use one container to receive new elements in their natural order, and a second to reverse that order only when the reversed order is actually needed, not on every single operation.

slides.sectionTitle: Implementing a queue with two stacks
slides.subTitle: An in-stack and an out-stack
slides.markdown:
A stack only gives you LIFO access, but a queue needs FIFO — the trick is using **two** stacks to reverse order twice, which cancels out back to the original order.

Everything new gets pushed onto an **in-stack**. To dequeue (get the oldest element), pop everything off the in-stack and push it onto an **out-stack** — that single transfer reverses the order, putting the oldest in-stack element on top of the out-stack. Pop from the out-stack to dequeue. As long as the out-stack still has elements, keep popping from it directly; only refill it from the in-stack once it's empty.

slides.sectionTitle: Enqueue and dequeue for a two-stack queue
Why each element moves at most twice
slides.subTitle: The amortized O(1) argument
slides.markdown:
Every element gets pushed onto the in-stack exactly once (on enqueue), and transferred from in-stack to out-stack **at most once** (it either gets transferred, or it's dequeued directly without ever needing to be — but never both, and never more than once either way). Then it gets popped off the out-stack exactly once (on dequeue).

So across the element's entire lifetime, it's touched a constant number of times — at most 3 total operations (push to in, transfer to out, pop from out) — regardless of how many *other* dequeue calls happen while it's waiting. Summing that constant-per-element cost over n elements gives O(n) total work for n operations, which is exactly what "O(1) amortized per operation" means: not that every single call is cheap, but that the total cost over a long sequence divided by the number of calls is a constant.

slides.sectionTitle: Implementing a stack using two queues

slides.subTitle: Which operation absorbs the O(n) cost
slides.markdown:
| | Two-stack queue | Single-queue-with-rotation stack |
|---|---|---|
| Cheap operation | enqueue: O(1) always | pop: O(1) always |
| Expensive operation | dequeue: O(1) amortized (occasional O(n) transfer) | push: O(n) every single time |
| Cost distribution | amortized — expensive step is rare | non-amortized — expensive step is every call |

The two structures differ in an important way beyond "which operation is expensive": the two-stack queue's expensive dequeue is **amortized** — most calls are cheap, and the O(n) transfer happens rarely enough that the *average* cost per call is still O(1). The single-queue stack's expensive push happens on **every** call, with no amortization — it's genuinely O(n) per operation, all the time, not just in the worst case.

That makes them meaningfully different despite looking symmetric: one design has a good average-case story, the other doesn't.

slides.subTitle: Instead of recognizing the amortized cost
slides.markdown:
A common mistake when analyzing the two-stack queue: looking at the dequeue method, seeing a `while` loop that can run up to n times, and concluding "dequeue is O(n)" without qualification.

That's true for a **single** dequeue call in the worst case, but it's the wrong lens for evaluating the structure overall — over any sequence of n enqueues and n dequeues, the total work across all dequeues combined is O(n), because each element is transferred from in-stack to out-stack at most once in its entire lifetime, not once per dequeue call. Reporting "O(n) per dequeue" without the amortized qualifier misrepresents how the structure actually performs under sustained use, and misses exactly the insight the question is testing for.

The fix is always to say both numbers: "O(n) worst case for a single call, O(1) amortized across a sequence of calls" — that pairing is the complete, correct answer.

slides.subTitle: It tests amortized reasoning, not just implementation
slides.markdown:
The implementation itself — two stacks, careful transfer logic — is straightforward once seen; most candidates can write it after a hint. What separates a strong answer is the complexity analysis: correctly identifying that a worst-case-looking O(n) operation is actually O(1) amortized, and being able to *prove* it (each element moves a bounded number of times, not "it usually works out").

This is a deliberately chosen proxy for a broader skill: recognizing when a locally expensive operation is globally cheap because of how rarely it triggers relative to how much cheap work surrounds it — the same reasoning that justifies dynamic array resizing, hash table rehashing, and union-find's path compression. Getting comfortable with this one example pays off well beyond queue/stack interconversion itself.
